verdict.content_summary: A dense postmortem by Teknium (Nous Research) on running their open-source Hermes coding agent to refactor its own 1M+ line Python codebase: a /goal standing objective drove a 19-hour run that dispatched 1,393 subagents (218 concurrent) across git worktrees in a 3-level delegation tree, all in one local Python process with remote inference. The orchestrator partitioned the code into 36 non-overlapping groups, generated written worker briefs from the objective plus an auto-accumulated Markdown skill document capturing months of the author's procedures and verification habits, and verified via byte-for-byte CLI --help diffs, identical tool JSON schemas, and commit-per-verified-step. Result: 34.4% non-test line reduction, god files broken up, ~$25k in model spend vs a $150k–$1.8M manual estimate, and a token-per-lookup metric (2,218 → 993) quantifying context-efficiency gains. Honest failure accounting: provider token expiry mid-run handled by a separate diagnostic session preparing a resume handoff, and community review catching regressions the tests missed (removed plugin-importable names, a suppress() rewrite changing exception handling at ~65 sites).

grabs.what: The auto-written Markdown skill document ('hermes-agent-dev') that accumulates the author's procedures, corrections, and verification habits across sessions and gets distributed to other engineers' setups
grabs.why: This is the single most portable idea for a markdown-first builder: your agents should maintain their own plain-text skill files in your existing pipeline, recording what worked and what you corrected, so the next task or agent starts with that context. It slots directly into a markdown-in/structured-queues-out ingest flow with zero new infrastructure.

grabs.what: Worktree fan-out orchestration: git worktrees as per-worker isolation, non-overlapping partition briefs (interfaces to preserve, required checks), and a coordinator-only top agent with hierarchical delegation
grabs.why: Directly portable to their local coding agents without buying anything — git worktrees are free, and the brief format (code to simplify, interfaces to preserve, required checks) is a structured in/out contract that matches their 'data is for machines' value. The single-Python-process + 64GB desktop + remote inference setup also validates their cheap-beats-fancy instinct.

grabs.what: Verification harness: byte-for-byte comparison of CLI --help output and tool JSON schemas before/after, commit after each verified step, and a separate agent session diagnosing crashes and preparing resume-from-commits handoffs
grabs.why: Steals cleanly into any of their agent pipelines: behavioral diffing of deterministic outputs is a cheap regression net for automated changes, commit-per-verified-step gives free crash recovery, and the diagnose-then-handoff pattern turns a killed run into a resumable one — all mechanisms, no product.

grabs.what: Hermes Agent itself (open-source, self-hostable coding agent with /goal standing-objective mode)
grabs.why: Fits their stack on paper — open-source, BYO-inference, runs on modest local hardware with remote models via their existing OpenRouter-style routing. Caveat: the headline $25k Claude run is not their budget, and they likely already have a coding agent; adopt for the /goal loop and skill-file system rather than as a replacement.

aspects: Standing-objective loop: a command that converts one-shot task completion into a persistent goal the agent keeps working toward without stopping for permission
Auto-accumulating skill file: the agent records procedures, corrections, and verification habits in a Markdown doc that compounds across tasks and engineers
Worktree fan-out: git worktrees as cheap isolation for parallel agents, with written briefs specifying interfaces-to-preserve and required checks per partition
Coordinator-only top agent: hierarchical delegation where the root handles routing exclusively and workers may spawn sub-workers
Behavioral diff verification: byte-for-byte comparison of deterministic outputs (CLI help, JSON schemas) as a refactor regression net, with a commit after each verified step
Crash handoff: a separate agent session diagnoses the failure and prepares a resume-from-saved-commits brief instead of restarting
Token-per-lookup metric: simulated symbol lookups (4,000) before/after to quantify a refactor's context-window efficiency, not just line counts
Human review as the net for what tests miss: community reviewers caught semantic regressions (removed public names, exception-handling rewrites) invisible to automated checks

finds.name: contextcost
finds.what_it_is: Python CLI (MIT, on PyPI) that measures what a repository costs an AI coding agent to read in tokens, identifies what is wasting that context budget, and re-measures after changes to prove the saving.
finds.different_angle: Shares the postmortem's token-per-lookup mechanism (2,218 → 993) — quantifying whether a refactor actually improved LLM readability — but productizes it as a reusable static-analysis tool rather than an ad-hoc metric computed once inside a 19-hour run.
finds.why_relevant_to_profile: Exactly the profile's taste: small single-purpose Python CLI, MIT, no cloud, structured measurement in/out. Slots into their refactor pipelines as a cheap local gate so codebase changes are judged on context-efficiency, not vibes.

finds.name: Shard
finds.what_it_is: Apache-2.0 Python orchestrator that decomposes a natural-language coding task into a DAG of parallel subtasks and executes them concurrently in isolated git worktrees, with TDD as the feedback loop.
finds.different_angle: Shares the coordinator-worker + worktree-isolation mechanism (1,393 subagents across worktrees) but at hobbyist scale: an LLM-planned task DAG instead of a 3-level delegation tree, and test-driven verification per subtask instead of byte-for-byte CLI/schema diffs.
finds.why_relevant_to_profile: A self-hostable, open-source analog of the Hermes orchestrator the profile could run against their own code; natural-language prompt in, parallel branches/commits out fits their structured-pipeline preference.

finds.name: etch
finds.what_it_is: Go CLI (MIT) for zero-config API change detection: record real API responses, diff them across versions or deploys, and approve changes — explicitly without writing tests.
finds.different_angle: Shares the postmortem's behavioral-verification mechanism (byte-for-byte CLI --help diffs, identical tool JSON schemas) but generalizes it to any interface: snapshot real outputs and diff them, catching the class of regression tests missed — like the suppress() rewrite that changed exception handling at ~65 sites.
finds.why_relevant_to_profile: Single-purpose, composable CLI they can wire into agent pipelines as a verification gate; the record → diff → approve flow produces machine-readable evidence per step, matching their commit-per-verified-step discipline.

finds.name: Cog
finds.what_it_is: MIT-licensed plain-text memory layer (375 stars) you clone once and point all your agents at — one centralized markdown memory shared across tools and projects instead of per-tool silos.
finds.different_angle: Shares the auto-accumulated Markdown skill-document mechanism (months of procedures and verification habits injected into worker briefs) but inverts it: a curated, persistent, cross-agent memory you maintain and version, rather than a skill doc auto-generated per run.
finds.why_relevant_to_profile: Plain-text-first, no database, no cloud, no account — precisely the profile's stack. Gives their local agent fleet a shared memory they can read, edit by hand, and track in git.

finds.name: Cairn
finds.what_it_is: Apache-2.0 append-only journal for AI agents living in a project's .agent/ directory — a git-like shared log of goals, decisions, tasks, and knowledge that persists across sessions and between agents.
finds.different_angle: Shares the markdown-memory mechanism but aims it at the multi-agent coordination problem the postmortem solved with written briefs: parallel agents read what the others just did instead of re-deriving state, via an append-only journal rather than a rewritten document.
finds.why_relevant_to_profile: For their multi-agent local setup, a shared append-only log in plain files (no DB, no account) is a portable coordination mechanism — including the resume-handoff pattern the postmortem needed when provider token expiry killed a run mid-flight.

Deprioritized: lantisprime/episodic-memory (252 open issues vs 3 stars — likely issue spam) and kunalkaiser/agentmemory (fork requiring the iii-engine). Kept five finds that each port one mechanism from the postmortem — context-cost metrics, worktree DAG orchestration, output-diff verification, curated markdown memory, and shared append-only agent journals — as small self-hostable tools.
